# What Stripe publishable keys the library redacts, and what it leaves alone.
#
# Every key here is built from the ordered run 0123456789abcdef, which no real
# credential is, written out until it is the twenty-four characters the pattern
# holds a body to. That count is a floor and not an abbreviation: a body
# shortened for readability would leave a case holding no key at all. One case
# carries the ninety-nine characters Stripe issues today, to say that the floor
# is not a count.
#
# Stripe's own table of key types carries a column reading safe to expose, and
# the publishable key is the one row where it reads yes: the key is embedded in
# the page it initializes, so a reader who has one has taken nothing. It is a
# pattern of its own for that reason. A caller masking a frontend bundle or a
# browser console log has no reason to redact a value that belongs there, and a
# caller masking a configuration dump they are about to share may want it gone;
# the two reach for different patterns and get what they asked for. The
# restricted, secret and organization keys are the other half of the format and
# have a corpus file of their own.
#
# The two cases under the over-match heading are not keys and nobody issued
# them. What they hold is a name whose first segment ends in pk, whose second is
# a mode and whose third is long enough to be a body, which is the whole of what
# the pattern asks for.

patterns: stripe-publishable-key

# The two modes, which is the whole of what a publishable key is written in.

case:     a live publishable key in an environment assignment
in:       STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=«stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a sandbox publishable key
in:       pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a publishable key in a client side configuration object
in:       {"publishableKey":"pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567","locale":"auto"}
out:      {"publishableKey":"«stripe-publishable-key»","locale":"auto"}

case:     a publishable key in the script that initializes a page with it
in:       const stripe = Stripe('pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567');
out:      const stripe = Stripe('«stripe-publishable-key»');

# How long a body is, which is the one count this pattern reads, and it is the
# floor the secret keys are held to because it is the same format. Twenty-four
# characters is the shortest body Stripe has printed in its own documentation:
# the ninety-nine characters it issues today are redacted whole, and so would a
# length neither Stripe nor a ruleset states be. What the floor holds back is
# the placeholder a template carries where a key goes, which for a publishable
# key is written into documentation far more often than a key is.
#
# What it leaves over is the key cut short. A line cut to a column limit partway
# through one leaves a prefix and a body too short to be a body, and every
# random character written before the cut comes through in the clear.

case:     the length Stripe issues today
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef012
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a body one character longer than the floor
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567z
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a key one character short of the floor
in:       STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_0123456789abcdef0123456
out:      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_0123456789abcdef0123456

case:     a key cut off at its prefix
in:       STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_
out:      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_

case:     a placeholder where a key goes
in:       STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_yourkeyhere
out:      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_yourkeyhere

# The mode. It is read as one of the names Stripe writes rather than as any
# lowercase word at all, which is what makes the anchor eight characters instead
# of the three a key type is. What that wagers is a mode Stripe has not written
# yet.

case:     a mode no Stripe page names
in:       pk_prod_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      pk_prod_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a key type with no mode behind it
in:       pk_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      pk_0123456789abcdef01234567

# The alphabet a body is written in: the letters of both cases and the ten
# digits. Neither the underscore nor the hyphen is in it, so either of them ends
# a body where it stands and what is left in front of it is too short to be one.

case:     a body written in capitals
in:       pk_live_0123456789ABCDEF01234567
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     an underscore in the body
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef_01234567
out:      pk_live_0123456789abcdef_01234567

case:     a hyphen in the body
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef-01234567
out:      pk_live_0123456789abcdef-01234567

# What a key may be written against. The byte in front of a prefix may be no
# letter and no digit, which is the demand the secret keys are held to and is
# read from the same declaration. Fewer words close on this key type than on
# those, but topk_ does — it is how the top-k operation is spelled in a name —
# so topk_live_ carries a whole prefix and is turned away by the letter in front
# of it. It would be kept even where it bought nothing, because the two halves
# of one format may not disagree about where a key may begin.
#
# Behind the key the redaction reaches to the end of the run, which is the price
# of reading a floor rather than a count. A letter or a digit written straight
# after a key is redacted with it; an underscore, a hyphen, a space or a quote
# ends the run and stays.

case:     a key after an underscore
in:       STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY_pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY_«stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a key after a letter
in:       xpk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      xpk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a key after a digit
in:       1pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      1pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a snake_case name closing on the publishable key type
in:       the topk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567 fixture was rebuilt
out:      the topk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567 fixture was rebuilt

case:     a key at the end of a sentence
in:       the key is pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567.
out:      the key is «stripe-publishable-key».

case:     a key before a word
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567suffix
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a key before an underscore, which ends the run
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567_suffix
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»_suffix

# The other half of Stripe's format, which this pattern leaves alone. That is
# the boundary between the two: Stripe's safe to expose column reads no for
# every one of these three and yes for the key above.

case:     a secret key
in:       STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a restricted key
in:       rk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      rk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     an organization key
in:       sk_org_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      sk_org_0123456789abcdef01234567

# Two keys written together. A key opens only where no letter and no digit
# stands in front of it, and everything a span covers is one or the other but
# for the underscores of the prefix — so the second would open nothing, were the
# byte in front the whole of the rule. It is not: a candidate opening in front
# has a whole body of the characters a body is written in behind it, which is a
# key and not a word. A secret key leaves one behind it as much as these do, so
# a publishable key written against one is read as well.
# builtin_stripe_secret_key.go argues it.

case:     two keys separated by a space
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567 pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      «stripe-publishable-key» «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a key written straight onto the end of another
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     a key written straight onto the end of a secret key
in:       sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567«stripe-publishable-key»

case:     an underscore between a secret key and one of these
in:       sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567_pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      sk_live_0123456789abcdef01234567_«stripe-publishable-key»

# What this pattern redacts that nobody issued. A prefix carries two
# underscores, so no base64 payload holds one and no digest does; what is left
# is text somebody wrote — a name whose first segment ends in pk, whose second
# is a mode, and whose third is twenty-four unbroken letters and digits.
#
# That is the answer rather than a fault in it: such a name is a key's format
# exactly, so nothing is left in the text to read the two apart by, and the only
# tightening on offer is the count, which the pattern's own file weighs and
# reads as a floor for the reason a wrong count costs a whole credential.

case:     a name whose segments spell a prefix, with a digest behind it
in:       pk_live_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
out:      «stripe-publishable-key»

case:     the same name at the start of a shell word
in:       cat pk_test_0123456789abcdef01234567.json
out:      cat «stripe-publishable-key».json

# And what this pattern leaves alone. The first two are the prefix: read in its
# own case, and written with the underscores Stripe writes rather than the
# hyphens the Anthropic and OpenAI keys carry. The digest carries no underscore
# and so holds no prefix to be found at, and no word of prose is spelled
# pk_live_.

case:     an uppercase prefix
in:       PK_LIVE_0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      PK_LIVE_0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     hyphens where the prefix carries underscores
in:       pk-live-0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      pk-live-0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a run of the right length opening with no prefix
in:       0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     a hexadecimal digest
in:       sha1=0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
out:      sha1=0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567

case:     prose
in:       there is no credential in this sentence
out:      there is no credential in this sentence
